description: A dense, many-stemmed shrub with tiny needle-like leaves in bundles along stiff, upright branches, and clusters of small white flowers at the tips in early summer; 1.2-2.4 m tall here. It is the most common chaparral shrub in California, forming thick stands on hot, dry slopes with thin soil, where it resprouts from a woody burl after fire and gives cover to quail, brush rabbits and wrentits.

season_notes.winter: Evergreen: winter rain brings new shoots, and stands burned in recent years sprout from their burls.
season_notes.spring: Fresh green growth, then clusters of small white flowers at the branch tips (May-June).
season_notes.summer: The flowers fade to rust-brown; the resinous leaves dry out, and chamise is one of the most flammable plants in the chaparral.
season_notes.fall: Rust-brown seed heads still cap the stems while the shrubs wait out the dry season for the first rain.

notes: The commonest chaparral shrub in California; dense, even stands on dry slopes. 0.6-3.5 m, here 1.2-2.4 m. Many slender stems rise from a basal burl (lignotuber), from which it resprouts after fire: stems 6-10 spreading about 22 degrees, thin (dbh/height 0.02). Stiff, upright, twiggy branchlets (one dense branch level, steep down angle, upward tropism). Bark grey-brown and shreddy on old stems. Leaves 4-10 mm, linear and needle-like, in bundles (fascicles) on short spur shoots, so the foliage is a fine dark-to-grey-green texture rather than leaves you can see: leaf_shape 'needle_fascicle'. Colour by season: darkest and greenest after winter rain, cream-tinged in late spring when dense terminal panicles of small white flowers open (May-June), greyer and dustier through the summer drought, rusty brown in fall from the dried flower heads. The architectural model is provisional: branching is sympodial with terminal inflorescences, which fits Leeuwenberg's model, but the basitonic, resprouting multi-stem habit is the stronger visual cue and is carried by trunk.stems. Needs a botanist's check.
